title: Petra and the Cellar
premise: Folklorist Isandro Zhou returns to the village of Petra to record its songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any verse twice—and to find his childhood imaginary friend, the pale figure called the Cellar-Keeper, waiting on his porch, unchanged after twenty years. As Isandro transcribes the forbidden songs, he realizes they are instructions for a half-finished ritual the village founders abandoned, one that binds a 'remembered one'—a person the village agreed to forget—to keep the harvest from failing. Isandro was that person, erased from every record and memory except the Cellar-Keeper's, who has loved him faithfully through the forgetting. To survive the rising harvest moon, Isandro must choose between completing the ritual, which would restore him to the village but unmake his friend, or breaking the ritual entirely, which frees them both but leaves the village to face what it buried. In the end, Isandro and the Cellar-Keeper finish the founders' work together, rewriting the song's final verse so that remembering and love are no longer opposites.
about_author: Jonah Nakamura is the pen name of a former archivist of oral traditions who spent three years collecting folk songs in remote mountain villages before turning to fiction. Their work explores what communities choose to forget, and what refuses to be forgotten.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Its Doors
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He arrives in Petra at dusk, checking doorways and counting windows out of old habit, and unpacks his recording equipment in his late grandmother's house. The village is warm but oddly careful with him. Emotional beat: the unease of homecoming to a place that feels like it's been expecting someone else.

chapters.title: A Song You Only Sing Once
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At the tavern, an old woman sings a harvest song for him, then goes white when he asks her to repeat the third verse. The room empties. The innkeeper warns him, gently, that songs here are sung once. Emotional beat: first crack in the village's polite surface.

chapters.title: The Figure on the Porch
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Waking at 3 a.m., he finds the Cellar-Keeper—a tall, pale figure from his childhood imaginings—sitting on the porch, unchanged, patient. It doesn't speak, only watches, and the porch light gutters. Emotional beat: terror braided with an awful, familiar comfort.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In the parish archive he searches for records of his own family and finds his grandmother's ledger altered: pages about a 'remembered one' cut out, his own childhood entries missing. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering your past has been edited.

chapters.title: The Founders' Hymn
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, with a flashback to childhood. He pieces together the founders' hymn from fragments and recognizes it as the song the tavern refused to repeat. The hymn's structure is a ritual: call, binding, forgetting, and a final verse that was never written. Emotional beat: scholarly dread turning to personal stakes.

chapters.title: Vera Remembers Nothing
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera Osei, the village schoolteacher who half-remembers a boy who isn't in any photo, dreams of a cellar door and wakes with dirt under her nails. She begins asking quiet questions. Emotional beat: the ache of a memory with no object.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He finally opens the cellar his grandmother kept locked and finds it larger inside than the house, walls scratched with tally marks and a child's drawings of a pale friend. The Cellar-Keeper waits at the bottom of the stairs. Emotional beat: the imaginary friend becomes terrifyingly real.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Waiting
chapters.summary: The Cellar-Keeper's POV. It explains, without words at first, that it has kept the ritual's half-light burning since Isandro was taken away, that the village forgot him to save the harvest, and that it refused to forget. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness—the first proof that Isandro was loved all along.

chapters.title: The Village That Agreed
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera confronts the eldest villagers, who admit in fragments that the founders bound a child to the cellar and then 'laid him down' from memory. Some are relieved he's back; others begin to fear what his return means for the harvest. Emotional beat: communal guilt surfacing like a drowned body.

chapters.title: Songs as Instructions
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Decoding the hymn, Isandro realizes each verse is a stage of the ritual and that the harvest moon in three weeks is the deadline. The unwritten final verse was meant to either release the remembered one or renew the forgetting. Emotional beat: cold clarity—he is inside a clock.

chapters.title: The First Verse Fails
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He attempts the ritual's opening verse alone in the cellar; the candles invert, the tally marks bleed, and something older than the Cellar-Keeper stirs below. He barely escapes. Emotional beat: the ritual is not a door but a mouth.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Keeps
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera follows Isandro's questions to the founders' original site in the orchard and finds a second, older cellar—the first binding, with the bones of a previous remembered one. Emotional beat: horror that this has happened before, and will again.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. As the moon waxes, crops fail early and the villagers split: some want to complete the ritual with Isandro as the sacrifice, others want him gone before the moon rises. His door is marked with chalk. Emotional beat: the community that erased him now hunts him.

chapters.title: A Name Spoken Twice
chapters.summary: The Cellar-Keeper's POV. It teaches Isandro that names spoken twice in the old tongue can't be forgotten again—but speaking his own name twice will also bind him to the cellar forever. Emotional beat: love offered with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: Vera's Choice
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera, whose half-memory makes her the only villager who can carry Isandro's name into the ritual, agrees to help, defying the elders. She and Isandro grow close, and the Cellar-Keeper watches with something like jealousy. Emotional beat: loyalty, and the first friction of a triangle.

chapters.title: The Elders' Confession
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The eldest villager confesses the full history: the founders bound the first remembered one out of desperation, and every generation since has renewed the forgetting rather than face the thing beneath the cellar. Emotional beat: pity for the perpetrators, and the weight of inherited sin.

chapters.title: What Waits Beneath
chapters.summary: The Cellar-Keeper's POV. It reveals the truth of its own origin: it is the previous remembered one, transformed by centuries in the half-light, and the 'thing below' is what remains of the first. Emotional beat: the beloved friend was once a sacrificed child.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Eve
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. On the eve, the village gathers at the orchard cellar with torches, split between mob and congregation. Isandro, Vera, and the Cellar-Keeper descend with the hymn half-sung. Emotional beat: the held breath before the plunge.

chapters.title: The Unwritten Verse
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In the deep cellar, the first remembered one rises, wearing the founders' faces, and demands the old bargain: a name for the harvest. Isandro begins the unwritten verse—his own composition—refusing both forgetting and sacrifice. Emotional beat: defiance at the edge of annihilation.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Song
chapters.summary: The Cellar-Keeper's POV. The ritual falters until the Cellar-Keeper speaks Isandro's name twice, binding itself to him instead, and Vera carries the new verse back to the villagers, who—some weeping, some raging—sing it once. Emotional beat: love paying duty's debt.

chapters.title: The Verse Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The new verse holds: the thing below dissolves, the harvest moon passes, and the village wakes remembering Isandro fully—his childhood, his grandmother, his name. The Cellar-Keeper, freed from its duty, begins to age like a person. Emotional beat: grief and joy arriving in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Song We Sing Again
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, coda. A year later, Isandro records the harvest song and the villagers sing it twice, willingly, with a new final verse of his making. The Cellar-Keeper—now simply a man with a name Isandro gave him—sits on the porch as the recorder turns. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace; memory and love reconciled.
